paras: The threatened lynching of David McMillan took place at the jail in Greenfield, Massachusetts, on the evening of December 6, 1881, when a crowd tried to seize McMillan, who was accused of shooting the parish priest, Father McCarthy. Officers holding the prisoner displayed revolvers, the crowd fell back, and McMillan was lodged in jail unharmed. Wire reports of the scene, under headings such as "Fear of Lynching" and "Safe in Jail", ran in papers across the country.

According to a Springfield dispatch, McMillan's wife had left him several years earlier and had lately become housekeeper for Father McCarthy, the Catholic parish priest at Greenfield. Refused admittance at the parsonage, McMillan was said to have returned three times, rung the bell violently and kicked the door, and then shot the priest twice when he answered. The first report placed the shooting on a Saturday night, while later Greenfield dispatches said Sunday evening.

McMillan reached Greenfield by rail at 6:45 on the evening of December 6 in the charge of Officer Fitzgerald. Because an attempt to lynch him by "enraged parishioners" was feared, the Fitchburg road allowed the train to stop about one hundred rods below the depot, and the officers drove the prisoner to the jail by carriage. Word of the plan had leaked out, however, and the yard before the jail was crowded with people anxious to get at him.

The crowd closed around the carriage shouting "Pull him out!" and "Shoot the villain!", but the officers' revolvers deterred it from using force. A committee from the Catholic church helped the officers keep order and guard the prisoner. The New Haven Morning Journal and Courier described McMillan as so frightened that he dragged the officer he was handcuffed to up the jail steps.

McMillan was to be examined at the jail before Trial Justice Thompson on a charge of intent to kill. Father McCarthy died about midnight after making a dying declaration about the assault, and a warrant charging McMillan with murder was then issued. Several thousand people attended the priest's funeral at Greenfield on December 9, conducted by Bishop O'Reilly.

No arrests of anyone in the crowd were reported, and no report of McMillan's examination or of a trial appears in the coverage. A Rhode Island weekly reported that McMillan claimed the shooting was in self-defence.

The only detailed account was a Greenfield dispatch printed by the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier on December 7 under the heading "Father McCarthy's Assailant—Lodged in Greenfield Jail." A shorter wire dated December 7 ran the next day in papers from Memphis and Knoxville to Dallas, Chicago, Salt Lake City and Los Angeles, and later in weeklies in Montana and Pennsylvania. Most versions put the threat in the headline, as in the Memphis Public Ledger's "Anxious to Lynch" and the Rock Island Argus's "Safe in Jail."

The papers treated the officers' success in getting the prisoner to jail as the news and called McMillan the priest's "murderer" before any hearing. None of them commented on the crowd, and none gave the race of McMillan or of the people in the jail yard. Copy errors spread with the wire: the Dallas Herald datelined the story "Greenville, Miss.", the Memphis paper named the prisoner "Daniel McMillen", and the Chicago Tribune dated the shooting "last Monday." Two weeks later the Mineral Point Tribune still reported that citizens "throng the yard and threaten a lynching."

Accounts differ on the day of the shooting: the first Springfield wire implied Saturday night, the Greenfield dispatches said Sunday, and the Chicago Tribune alone said Monday. The account of McMillan kicking at the door before firing came from the early wire, while the self-defence claim was reported only in the Rhode Island weekly, without detail.

bases: A crowd filled the Greenfield jail yard to seize and lynch a prisoner charged with shooting a priest and was held back by armed officers (A3, A6, A7); no one was harmed, so it is a threatened lynching.

A crowd in the jail yard shouted to pull out and shoot McMillan, who was accused of shooting Father McCarthy, but the officers' revolvers deterred them and he was jailed unharmed (A3, A6). No one was killed, so the episode is a threatened lynching, not a lynching.

Every account of the crowd comes from Greenfield dispatches of Dec. 6-7 that share their wording ('driven rapidly to jail', 'anxious to get at the prisoner') and were reprinted nationally (A3, A6, A7, A10); no independent local or later account was found.

accounts.label: Greenfield dispatch, Dec. 6
accounts.gist: The officers stopped the train short of the depot to avoid a feared lynching; a crowd in the jail yard closed around the carriage shouting to pull him out and shoot him, but the officers' revolvers and a Catholic church committee kept order.

accounts.label: Wire report, Dec. 7
accounts.gist: The jail yard was crowded with people 'anxious to lynch' the prisoner, but a display of revolvers by the officers prevented violence; the priest died about midnight and a murder warrant was issued.

accounts.label: McMillan's claim, as reported

framing.detail: Papers from Tennessee to Montana ran the Dec. 7 wire under heads such as 'Fear of Lynching', 'Anxious to Lynch' and 'SAFE IN JAIL', treating the officers' success as the news and calling McMillan the priest's 'murderer'.
The New Haven Morning Journal and Courier gave the fullest local detail, describing 'enraged parishioners' and McMillan's terror, without comment on the crowd.

conflicts.note: The first Springfield wire, dated Dec. 4, says 'last night'; the Dec. 7 Greenfield wires say Sunday; the Chicago Tribune's 'last Monday' stands alone. The jail scene itself was the evening of Dec. 6 in all versions.
Spelling variants of one man; 'Daniel' appears only in the Memphis reprint.
The Dallas Herald's 'Greenville, Miss.' carries the same text as the Greenfield wire and is a misprint.

No paper gives McMillan's race (or anyone's); nothing ties the episode to anti-Black violence.
Threatened: the crowd closed around the carriage shouting, but the officers' revolvers 'deterred them from any actual application of force'.
Gathering in the jail yard and threats; no pursuit is reported, no siege of the jail, and only the officers are reported armed.
The jail scene was the evening of Dec. 6; Dec. 7 is the wire dateline; the shooting was Dec. 3 or 4.
